question: Under the Navigation Rules, may a boater add extra lights near the required navigation lights just for decoration?
choice_a: Yes, any color of extra light may be added near the running lights with no restriction
choice_b: Extra deck or cabin lighting is prohibited on any boat at any time, decorative or not
choice_c: No -- a vessel must not exhibit any additional light that could be mistaken for a required navigation light, impair the visibility or distinctive character of a required light, or interfere with a proper lookout
choice_d: Only red decorative lights are restricted; every other color is unrestricted near navigation lights
explanation: The Navigation Rules prohibit exhibiting other lights that could be confused with, or that degrade the visibility of, the required navigation lights, or that could interfere with keeping a proper lookout.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 20

question: Under the Navigation Rules, when must a vessel display her day shapes, such as a ball, cone, or diamond?
choice_a: Day shapes are purely optional decorations with no requirement to display them
choice_b: Day shapes are required only at night, as a replacement for navigation lights
choice_c: Day shapes are required only on vessels over 65 feet in length
choice_d: During daylight hours, in all weathers, whenever the situation the shape represents (such as being anchored or restricted in her ability to maneuver) applies
explanation: Day shapes are the daytime equivalent of navigation lights and must be exhibited during daylight, in all weather conditions, whenever the situation they signal applies to the vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 20

question: What is the horizontal arc of visibility of a masthead light, and how is it mounted?
choice_a: 225 degrees, mounted along the vessel's fore-and-aft centerline so it shows an unbroken light from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side
choice_b: 360 degrees, the same arc used by an all-round light
choice_c: 135 degrees, centered on the vessel's stern
choice_d: 45 degrees, aimed straight up so it is visible to aircraft
explanation: A masthead light is defined as a white light over the fore-and-aft centerline showing an unbroken arc of 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 21(a)

question: What is the horizontal arc of visibility of each sidelight (red on port, green on starboard) under the Navigation Rules' definitions?
choice_a: 360 degrees, visible all the way around the vessel
choice_b: 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its respective side
choice_c: 225 degrees, identical to the arc of a masthead light
choice_d: Sidelights have no rule-defined arc and may be aimed in any direction
explanation: Each sidelight is defined as showing an unbroken arc of 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its own side of the vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 21(b)

question: What is the horizontal arc of visibility of a sternlight?
choice_a: 225 degrees, the same arc as a masthead light
choice_b: 360 degrees, the same arc as an all-round light
choice_c: 135 degrees, centered on the vessel's stern, 67.5 degrees on each side of dead astern
choice_d: A sternlight has no rule-defined arc
explanation: A sternlight is a white light placed as near the stern as practicable, showing an unbroken arc of 135 degrees centered on dead astern.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 21(c)

question: What does the Navigation Rules mean by an 'all-round light,' such as the light used to mark a vessel at anchor?
choice_a: A light that shines only toward the bow of the vessel
choice_b: A rotating light that sweeps like a lighthouse beam
choice_c: A light visible only from directly astern
choice_d: A light showing an unbroken arc of 360 degrees around the horizon
explanation: An all-round light is defined as showing an unbroken arc of the full 360 degrees of the horizon, which is why it is used for signals -- like an anchor light -- meant to be seen from any direction.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 21

question: On a vessel less than 12 meters in length, at what minimum distance must the sidelights and masthead light generally be visible to another vessel?
choice_a: Sidelights visible at least 1 nautical mile, and the masthead light visible at least 2 nautical miles
choice_b: Sidelights visible at least 10 nautical miles and the masthead light at least 20 nautical miles
choice_c: Both lights need only be visible from about 50 feet away
choice_d: Minimum visibility distance is not addressed by the Navigation Rules
explanation: For vessels under 12 meters, the Rules set minimum visibility ranges of about 1 nautical mile for sidelights and about 2 nautical miles for the masthead light, so the lights can be seen with enough time to react.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 22 -- minimum light visibility ranges by vessel length

question: A power-driven vessel less than 7 meters long whose maximum speed does not exceed 7 knots may, in place of full running lights, show what minimum lighting when underway at night?
choice_a: No lights are required at all for such a small, slow vessel
choice_b: An all-round white light, and sidelights too if practicable
choice_c: Only a single red light, with no white or green light required
choice_d: A single flashing amber light
explanation: A very small, slow power-driven vessel is permitted a simplified lighting arrangement -- an all-round white light, plus sidelights if practicable -- instead of the full masthead-sidelight-sternlight configuration.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 23 -- small, slow power-driven vessel exception

question: How can a boater at night generally distinguish a sailing vessel under sail alone from a power-driven vessel, based solely on their required lights?
choice_a: There is no lighting difference between a sailing vessel and a power-driven vessel
choice_b: A sailing vessel shows only a masthead light and no sidelights
choice_c: A sailing vessel under sail shows sidelights and a sternlight but no masthead light, while a power-driven vessel underway shows a masthead light in addition to sidelights and a sternlight
choice_d: A power-driven vessel is prohibited from ever showing a sternlight
explanation: The absence of a masthead light is the key visual cue: a sailing vessel under sail alone shows sidelights and a sternlight but not a masthead light, while a power-driven vessel underway must show a masthead light as well.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rules 23 and 25 -- distinguishing sail from power at night

question: What is a combined 'tricolor' lantern, sometimes used on sailing vessels less than 20 meters in length?
choice_a: A light that cycles through red, green, and white every second to attract attention
choice_b: A day shape, not a light, made of three colored balls
choice_c: A light required only on powerboats, never on sailboats
choice_d: A single lantern carried at or near the top of the mast that combines the sidelights and sternlight into one fixture, shown in place of separate lights
explanation: A sailing vessel under 20 meters may combine her sidelights and sternlight into a single tricolor lantern carried at or near the masthead, rather than using separate fixtures around the hull.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 25(b) -- combined lantern for small sailing vessels

question: In addition to (not instead of) her normal sidelights and sternlight, what optional identifying lights may a sailing vessel underway exhibit at or near the top of her mast?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over green
choice_b: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, white over red
choice_c: A single flashing blue light
choice_d: Sailing vessels are not permitted any additional lights under the Navigation Rules
explanation: A sailing vessel underway may optionally show two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over green, near the top of the mast, as an extra means of identifying herself as a sailing vessel -- but not together with a combined tricolor lantern.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 25(c) -- optional red-over-green masthead lights for sailing vessels

question: What must a person rowing or paddling a small vessel at night have ready at hand if the vessel does not carry the lights prescribed for sailing vessels?
choice_a: Nothing -- vessels under oars or paddle are exempt from all lighting rules
choice_b: An electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, ready to be shown in time to prevent collision
choice_c: A full masthead light identical to a power-driven vessel's
choice_d: A continuously burning red flare
explanation: A vessel under oars that does not carry sailing-vessel lights must at least have a white light, such as a flashlight or lantern, ready to show in time to avoid a collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 25(d) -- lights for vessels under oars

question: What light configuration identifies a vessel actively engaged in trawling (dragging a net through the water) at night?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over white
choice_b: A single flashing yellow light
choice_c: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, green over white
choice_d: The same lights as an ordinary power-driven vessel, with no distinguishing signal
explanation: A vessel engaged in trawling displays two all-round lights in a vertical line, green over white, distinguishing her from ordinary traffic and from other types of fishing vessels.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 26(b) -- lights for a trawling vessel

question: What light configuration identifies a vessel engaged in fishing other than trawling, such as with lines or pots?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, green over white
choice_b: A single all-round yellow light
choice_c: A single red masthead light
choice_d: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over white
explanation: A vessel fishing by methods other than trawling, such as with lines, nets, or traps, shows two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over white -- the reverse color order from a trawler.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 26(c) -- lights for a non-trawling fishing vessel

question: What lights identify a vessel that is 'not under command,' meaning she is temporarily unable to maneuver as the Rules require due to some exceptional circumstance?
choice_a: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line where they can best be seen, plus, by day, two black balls in a vertical line
choice_b: A single flashing green light
choice_c: The identical lights used for a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
choice_d: No special lights are required for a vessel not under command
explanation: A vessel not under command shows two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, and two black balls in a vertical line by day, warning other vessels that she cannot reliably maneuver to avoid them.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 27(a) -- lights/shapes for a vessel not under command

question: What lights and day shapes identify a vessel 'restricted in her ability to maneuver,' such as one laying cable or conducting dredging operations?
choice_a: Two all-round red lights, identical to a vessel not under command
choice_b: Three all-round lights in a vertical line -- red, white, red from top to bottom -- plus, by day, a ball, diamond, and ball in a vertical line
choice_c: A single flashing white strobe
choice_d: No distinguishing lights or shapes are used for this vessel type
explanation: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver shows a red-white-red vertical light combination at night, and a ball-diamond-ball day shape combination in daylight, distinct from the two-red-lights signal used for a vessel not under command.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 27(b) -- lights/shapes for a vessel restricted in ability to maneuver

question: When a dredging vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver has an obstruction on one side, how does she indicate which side is safe for another vessel to pass?
choice_a: A single yellow light always marks the safe side, regardless of which side the obstruction is on
choice_b: The vessel sounds one long horn blast to indicate the safe side rather than using lights or shapes
choice_c: Two all-round red lights (or two balls by day) mark the obstructed side, and two all-round green lights (or two diamonds by day) mark the side that is safe to pass
choice_d: There is no way to indicate which side is safe; boaters must simply avoid the vessel entirely
explanation: In addition to her restricted-maneuverability signal, a dredging vessel with an obstruction shows red lights or balls toward the blocked side and green lights or diamonds toward the side with safe passing room.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 27 -- dredging vessel obstruction-side signals

question: What lights or day shape identify a large vessel that is 'constrained by her draft,' meaning her deep draft severely limits her ability to deviate from a channel?
choice_a: A single green light shown forward
choice_b: The identical lights used for a vessel at anchor
choice_c: No special signal exists for a vessel constrained by her draft
choice_d: Three all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, or a cylinder shape by day
explanation: A vessel constrained by her draft shows three all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, or a cylinder day shape, warning other vessels she cannot safely leave the deep-water channel to give way.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 28 -- vessel constrained by draft

question: What lights identify a vessel actively engaged on pilotage duty?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line at or near the masthead, white over red, in addition to sidelights and a sternlight if underway
choice_b: A single flashing blue light, identical to a law enforcement vessel
choice_c: The same lights required for a vessel not under command
choice_d: Pilot vessels display no special lights under the Navigation Rules
explanation: A vessel engaged on pilotage duty shows a distinctive white-over-red all-round light combination at or near the masthead, along with normal running lights while underway.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 29 -- pilot vessel lights

question: For a vessel 50 meters or more in length, what additional anchor light is required beyond the light shown forward?
choice_a: A second anchor light is never required regardless of vessel size
choice_b: A second all-round white light shown aft, at a lower level than the forward light
choice_c: A red flashing light replacing the white forward light
choice_d: Two green lights instead of white
explanation: While a smaller anchored vessel may show a single all-round white light, a vessel 50 meters or more in length must show both a forward anchor light and a second, lower all-round white light near the stern.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 30 -- anchor lights for larger vessels

question: Is a vessel less than 7 meters in length always required to show an anchor light when anchored?
choice_a: Yes, every anchored vessel of any size must always show an anchor light with no exceptions
choice_b: No, no vessel under 20 feet is ever required to show any light under any circumstance
choice_c: No -- a vessel under 7 meters is not required to exhibit an anchor light unless she is anchored in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or other area where other vessels normally navigate
choice_d: Anchor lights are required only for sailing vessels, never for powerboats
explanation: The Navigation Rules exempt very small anchored vessels from the anchor light requirement, but only when they are anchored away from channels, fairways, anchorages, and other areas where other boat traffic normally passes.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 30 -- small vessel anchor light exemption

question: What day shape must an anchored vessel display where it can best be seen?
choice_a: A red cone
choice_b: Two black balls in a vertical line
choice_c: A striped orange flag
choice_d: One black ball
explanation: The daytime signal for a vessel at anchor is a single black ball shape displayed where it can best be seen, corresponding to the all-round white anchor light used at night.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 30 -- anchor ball day shape

question: What lights and day shapes must a vessel display in addition to her anchor light if she runs aground?
choice_a: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, and three black balls in a vertical line by day
choice_b: No additional lights or shapes are required beyond her normal anchor light
choice_c: A single flashing white strobe only
choice_d: The same signal used for a vessel not under command, with nothing further
explanation: A vessel aground must show her anchor light(s) plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, or three black balls in a vertical line by day, to distinguish her situation from a normally anchored vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 30 -- lights/shapes for a vessel aground

question: Is a vessel less than 12 meters in length that runs aground required to display the special aground lights and shapes (two red lights at night, three balls by day)?
choice_a: Yes, every vessel of any size that runs aground must display them with no exception
choice_b: No -- a vessel under 12 meters aground is not required to exhibit those particular aground lights or shapes
choice_c: Only sailing vessels under 12 meters are exempt; powerboats aground are not
choice_d: The exemption applies only during daylight hours, not at night
explanation: Small vessels under 12 meters that run aground are exempted from the additional two-red-lights and three-balls aground signal that larger vessels must display.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 30 -- small vessel aground exemption

question: What must a vessel 100 meters or more in length do at anchor at night, beyond showing her required anchor lights?
choice_a: Nothing further is required beyond the standard anchor light
choice_b: She must sound her horn continuously through the night
choice_c: Use available working or equivalent lights to illuminate her decks
choice_d: She must extinguish all other lighting to avoid confusing nearby vessels
explanation: A very large anchored vessel, 100 meters or more in length, must also illuminate her decks using available working or equivalent lighting, helping other vessels recognize her size and position.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 30 -- deck illumination for large anchored vessels

question: When anchoring, why should a boater generally approach the chosen spot slowly, head into the wind or current, and lower the anchor over the bow rather than the stern?
choice_a: The bow is used only because most anchors are too heavy to lift from the stern
choice_b: There is no safety reason for this; either end works identically in every condition
choice_c: Anchoring from the stern is required by federal law
choice_d: Approaching slowly and lowering the anchor over the bow lets it set properly as the boat drifts back, while anchoring from the stern in open water or current risks pulling the low transom under and swamping the boat
explanation: Boats are designed with more freeboard at the bow; anchoring from the stern in current or waves can pull the lower transom underwater, so the anchor should be set from the bow while the boat drifts or is eased back on the rode.
source_note: TPWD Boater Education Manual / NASBLA-aligned anchoring fundamentals -- anchoring from the bow

question: After lowering the anchor and letting out adequate scope, what should a boater do to help confirm the anchor is actually set and holding?
choice_a: Gently back down on the anchor line using the engine in reverse, checking that the boat is not dragging before leaving it unattended
choice_b: Immediately shut off the engine and go below without checking
choice_c: Motor forward at full throttle to test the anchor's strength
choice_d: There is no practical way to confirm an anchor is holding before leaving the boat
explanation: Backing down gently on the anchor line under power helps set the anchor into the bottom and lets the operator confirm, by checking against fixed landmarks, that the boat is not dragging before considering the anchor secure.
source_note: TPWD Boater Education Manual -- setting and testing the anchor

question: Why is it important to consider a boat's 'swing radius' -- the circle it can travel around its anchor as wind or current shifts -- when choosing where to anchor near other boats?
choice_a: Swing radius only matters for sailboats, not powerboats
choice_b: A boat anchored too close to others may swing into them or tangle anchor lines as conditions change, even if the boats appeared well spaced when first anchored
choice_c: Anchored boats do not move once the anchor is set, so swing radius is irrelevant
choice_d: Swing radius is a concern only in saltwater tides, never on Texas lakes or rivers
explanation: An anchored boat swings around its anchor as wind and current shift, so boaters must leave enough room between anchored vessels for that swing, or boats that looked well separated at first can collide or foul lines later.
source_note: TPWD Boater Education Manual / NASBLA-aligned anchoring fundamentals -- swing radius when anchoring near other vessels

question: What type of bottom generally provides the best holding power for a typical recreational anchor?
choice_a: Bare rock or thick grass, which grip an anchor more securely than mud or sand
choice_b: Bottom composition makes no difference to how well an anchor holds
choice_c: Firm mud or sand, into which most anchor designs can dig in and set securely
choice_d: Only bottoms covered in loose gravel provide good holding power
explanation: Most common recreational anchor designs are made to dig into and hold in firm mud or sand; grass, rock, and other hard or slick bottoms tend to give the anchor much poorer holding.
source_note: NASBLA-aligned anchoring fundamentals -- bottom type and anchor holding power

question: When retrieving (weighing) an anchor, what is a recommended technique rather than simply hauling on the line from a distance?
choice_a: Anchors should always be pulled from as far away as possible for the best leverage
choice_b: The anchor line should be cut and abandoned rather than retrieved, since re-setting an anchor is unsafe
choice_c: Retrieval technique has no bearing on effort or safety
choice_d: Motor slowly toward the anchor as the rode is taken in, using the boat's power to help break the anchor free once the boat is directly over it
explanation: Motoring slowly up to the anchor while taking in the rode, rather than trying to haul it from a distance and angle, makes it far easier to break the anchor free of the bottom and lift it aboard.
source_note: TPWD Boater Education Manual -- retrieving the anchor

question: Why do many recreational anchor rodes combine a length of chain near the anchor with nylon rope for the remainder of the rode?
choice_a: The chain resists abrasion on the bottom and adds weight that helps the anchor pull horizontally, while the nylon rope's stretch absorbs shock loads from wave and wind action
choice_b: Chain is used only because rope alone is never strong enough to hold any boat
choice_c: Combining chain and rope is purely a matter of cost, with no functional benefit
choice_d: Rope is placed nearest the anchor and chain nearest the boat, the reverse of standard practice
explanation: A short length of chain at the anchor end resists bottom abrasion and helps keep the pull angle low for better holding, while the nylon rope portion stretches to absorb shock loads, reducing strain on the anchor and cleat.
source_note: NASBLA-aligned anchoring fundamentals -- anchor rode composition (chain and rope)
